cases.abstract: Expanding a language model's context window does not necessarily improve its use of information within that window. We examine this distinction through multi-document question answering and synthetic key-value retrieval, changing the position of relevant information and the amount of distracting content while preserving the required answer. Question-answering accuracy generally peaks when the answer-bearing passage comes first or last and declines when it appears in the middle; in the worst tested placements, GPT-3.5-Turbo performs below its closed-book accuracy. Extended-context counterparts show little advantage when the inputs fit both models' windows. Several models exhibit similar positional weaknesses on random UUID retrieval, although both Claude variants perform nearly perfectly. Repeating the query before and after the data largely resolves synthetic retrieval errors but leaves question-answering positional sensitivity substantially unchanged. In a complementary open-domain evaluation, reader accuracy saturates before retrieval recall, limiting the benefit of additional documents. Together, these controlled contrasts show that accommodating more tokens and retrieving a matching value are insufficient indicators of effective evidence use in the evaluated question-answering settings.
cases.methods: Holding the question and answer evidence fixed while reordering documents makes position, rather than answer availability, the quantity under test. Each of 2,655 NaturalQuestions-Open queries with paragraph annotations is paired with its answer-bearing Wikipedia document and retrieved distractors that exclude the annotated answers. Moving that document within contexts of 10, 20, or 30 documents tests location sensitivity; changing the distractor count tests context length. Closed-book and single-document oracle prompts provide reference points for answering without supplied evidence and without distractor competition. A companion retrieval task uses serialized JSON with 75, 140, or 300 random UUID key-value pairs and 500 examples per setting. Removing most linguistic content tests whether positional difficulty persists in simple token matching. Both tasks use greedy decoding and count an output as correct when it contains an annotated answer or the requested value.
cases.results: Query repetition improves UUID retrieval without resolving the question-answering failure. With 300 key-value pairs, GPT-3.5-Turbo (16K) achieves perfect retrieval when the query precedes and follows the data, compared with 45.6% accuracy at the worst placement when the query appears only afterward. On multi-document question answering, the same change slightly improves accuracy when the answer document comes first but slightly lowers it elsewhere. Providing advance access to the query therefore helps locate a UUID value without establishing better use of natural-language evidence. Training-length comparisons further qualify the positional diagnosis: Flan-UL2's best-to-worst accuracy difference is only 1.9 percentage points within its 2,048-token training window, whereas longer inputs produce a middle-position disadvantage. GPT-3.5-Turbo and its 16K counterpart also have nearly identical positional profiles when both can accommodate the input. Together, the comparisons show why a larger supported window or a successful matching test alone cannot establish robust question answering across evidence positions.
cases.notes: Retain the diagnostic priority and original evidence selection. The abstract contrasts input capacity with usable evidence; Methods explains the fixed-answer positional control and UUID task; Results connects the query-placement intervention to its different task outcomes (Sections 2-4) and preserves the training-window condition. Claude's retrieval exception and the closed-book disadvantage remain. Architectural explanations are not treated as established causes. Omit the ambiguous greater-than-20% drop rather than infer a percentage-point change.

cases.abstract: Retrieval can supply relevant passages without ensuring that the generated claims are supported by them. Self-RAG makes this distinction operational by training a language model to predict retrieval decisions and judgments of passage relevance, evidential support, and response utility alongside its response text. A separate critic supplies reflection-token annotations offline, allowing the generator to perform these evaluations itself at inference. When retrieval is triggered, different passages condition competing sentence continuations, and predicted support contributes to their selection alongside relevance and generation scores. Zero-shot evaluations of 7B and 13B models cover six tasks spanning question answering, classification, biographies, and cited long-form answers. Compared with Llama2-FT7B, trained on the same instruction-output pairs but given retrieval only at test time, Self-RAG7B increases PopQA accuracy from 48.7% to 54.9%. On ASQA, its 13B model exceeds retrieval-augmented ChatGPT in citation precision but trails in citation recall and answer correctness. Increasing the support weight raises precision while lowering MAUVE fluency scores. The inference controls therefore make the trade-offs between attribution and other aspects of answer quality adjustable without retraining.
cases.methods: Self-RAG uses offline critique to make evidence judgments available during generation. A Llama 2-7B critic trained on GPT-4 feedback annotates instruction-output pairs with retrieval decisions and relevance, support, and utility tokens. The generator learns response text and these tokens through next-token prediction, while retrieved passages are masked from the loss. At inference, a threshold on the retrieval-token probability determines whether to request passages. If retrieval occurs, each passage conditions a separate candidate sentence; segment-level beam search ranks these continuations using generation scores plus a weighted sum of normalized critique-token probabilities. The predicted support score can therefore influence which claim is selected, rather than support being presumed from the availability of a relevant passage. Adjusting the support weight or retrieval threshold changes inference behavior without further training, and the separate critic is not needed for generation.
cases.results: Better citation support does not necessarily mean better answers in the same-data comparison. Relative to Llama2-FT7B, trained on the same instruction-output pairs without retrieved passages or reflection tokens but augmented with retrieval at test time, Self-RAG7B raises PopQA accuracy from 48.7% to 54.9% and ASQA citation precision from 5.0% to 66.9%. Yet ASQA answer correctness (str-em) decreases from 31.0% to 30.0%. Using the same five ASQA documents and a zero retrieval threshold, Self-RAG13B also exceeds retrieval-augmented ChatGPT in precision, 70.3% versus 65.1%, while trailing in recall, 71.3% versus 76.6%, and str-em, 31.7% versus 40.7%. Increasing the support weight in the 7B ASQA analysis raises citation precision but lowers MAUVE. Reducing retrieval frequency also hurts PopQA accuracy more than PubHealth accuracy. These results support tunable evidence selection and attribution, while showing that citation gains can coexist with losses in correctness, recall, or measured fluency.
cases.notes: Preserve the attribution-versus-correctness distinction rather than the source's blanket superiority wording. Methods makes the passage-conditioned selection rule recoverable (Sections 3.2-3.3); Results anchors the quality trade-offs in Table 2 and Section 5.2. The shared-data comparison evaluates the combined framework, not an isolated effect of reflection tokens. ASQA uses a zero retrieval threshold and shared five-document inputs. Main training uses 150k pairs; the 50k ablations and 150-example ASQA subset are not treated as full-test results. Critique predictions are learned judgments, not support guarantees; outputs can still contain unsupported claims.
